covers.quote: Place a comma after adverbs and other introductory words
You don’t need a comma after an introductory word if the sentence is very short.

rules.quote: Use a comma after introductory words, such as greetings and adverbs, or when addressing someone.
rules.specification: The manual does not define ‘very short’. A checker needs a reviewer-approved interpretation of that exception.
rules.violation_condition: An introductory word, greeting or address is not separated from the following sentence by a comma, outside the very-short-sentence exception.
when: Applies to introductory words, greetings and words addressing someone.
A comma may be omitted if the sentence is very short.
rules.why: G-4: use the actionable body wording; G-3: retain the very-short-sentence permission as an exception.

covers.quote: Use commas after adverbial phrases and adverbial clauses.
They should also have a comma after them if they start the sentence.
Use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral.
It doesn’t matter how short the sentence is.
If ‘for example’ begins a sentence, it is an introductory phrase. Follow it with a comma.
In these cases, you don’t need a comma before the phrase.

rules.quote: Use a comma after phrases and clauses that change the whole sentence
rules.violation_condition: An introductory phrase or clause is not separated from the main clause by a comma.
when: The phrase or clause introduces the sentence.
Includes conditional clauses beginning with words such as ‘if’, ‘unless’ or ‘until’.
Includes sentence-initial ‘for example’.
A comma is required between an introductory phrase ending with a numeral and an immediately following numeral, regardless of sentence length.
A phrase moved to the end of the sentence does not require a comma before it merely because it could have been introductory.
rules.why: G-2: introductory adverbial and conditional clauses and the numeral-boundary case are conditions of the same comma check.

covers.quote: Avoid this type of sentence structure because the string of numbers can be confusing.

rules.quote: Avoid beginning a sentence with a string of numbers and dates
rules.specification: Flag the illustrated construction: an introductory date or number phrase immediately followed by another numeral, even if a comma separates them. Do not flag every sentence that merely begins with a date.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence begins with an introductory numeric or date phrase followed immediately by another numeral, creating a confusing string of numbers.
when: An introductory phrase ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral.
rules.why: G-4: the body restates this readability rule; the separate comma requirement is absorbed into the introductory-phrase rule.

covers.quote: Set off non-essential clauses
Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.
If you can remove the clause and your sentence means the same thing, it’s non-essential and should go between commas.

rules.quote: Use commas around clauses that add information but aren’t essential to the meaning of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: A non-essential clause lacks its delimiting commas, or an essential clause is incorrectly set off with commas.
when: Use delimiting commas for clauses that add non-essential information.
Do not delimit a clause with commas if it is essential to the intended meaning.
A clause is non-essential if removing it leaves the intended main meaning unchanged.
rules.why: G-1: mark the specific child rather than the grouping parent; G-2: essential and non-essential clauses are cases of the same clause-delimiting check.

covers.quote: Place commas around nouns that define the same thing they follow
You should be able to take out the noun phrase between the comma pair and still have a grammatically correct sentence.

rules.quote: Use a pair of commas when you have 2 noun phrases next to each other that define the same thing.
rules.violation_condition: A supplementary noun phrase identifying the same thing as the preceding noun phrase is missing one or both delimiting commas.
when: Two adjacent noun phrases refer to the same thing and the second supplies non-essential information.
Removing the second noun phrase leaves a grammatically complete sentence.
rules.why: G-1: retain the specific apposition child; G-4: consolidate its heading and removal test.

covers.quote: Separate questions tagged onto a sentence

rules.quote: Use a comma before a question that is part of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: A question tag is attached to a sentence without a preceding comma.
when: A question tag is attached to the end of a sentence.
rules.why: G-1: question tags have their own specific check; G-4: use the actionable body sentence.

covers.quote: Use commas with the phrase ‘for example’

rules.quote: Generally, use a comma before and after the phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence.
rules.specification: The manual says ‘Generally’ without enumerating all exceptions. The stated introductory and bullet-list cases are handled separately.
rules.violation_condition: Parenthetical ‘for example’ within a sentence lacks a comma before or after it.
when: ‘For example’ is parenthetical within a sentence.
Sentence-initial use follows the introductory-phrase rule.
Use before a bullet list follows the colon rule.
rules.why: G-4: choose the specific body wording; G-2: distinguish medial use from introductory and bullet-list uses.

rules.quote: If you’re introducing a bullet list after ‘for example’, use a colon.
rules.violation_condition: A bullet-list lead-in ending in ‘for example’ lacks a colon after that phrase.
when: ‘For example’ introduces a bullet list.
rules.why: G-1: this is a distinct punctuation check, not a restatement of the surrounding comma rule.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas with Latin shortened forms

rules.quote: If you use Latin shortened forms, such as ‘e.g.’ and ‘i.e.’, don’t follow them with a comma.
rules.violation_condition: A Latin shortened form is immediately followed by a comma.
when: A Latin shortened form such as ‘e.g.’ or ‘i.e.’ is used.
rules.why: G-4: the body specifies the position of the prohibited comma more precisely than the heading.

covers.quote: Use commas to connect 2 or more principal clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’, ‘so’).
If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
The exception to this rule is when you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.

rules.quote: Place commas between principal clauses joined together with a conjunction
rules.violation_condition: Joined principal clauses lack a separating comma where their subjects differ, or a series of more than two shared-subject principal clauses lacks the required separating commas.
when: Principal clauses are joined by a coordinating conjunction such as ‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’ or ‘so’.
A comma is required before the conjunction when the clauses have different subjects.
Two clauses sharing one subject need neither a repeated subject nor a comma.
More than two principal clauses sharing one subject are separated with commas, including before the final conjunction.
rules.why: G-2: different subjects, a shared subject and more than two shared-subject clauses are conditions of one check.

rules.quote: Do not use this rule to create a sentence of more than 25 words.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence formed by joining principal clauses with commas and coordinating conjunctions contains more than 25 words.
when: The sentence connects principal clauses using commas and coordinating conjunctions.
rules.why: The instruction gives a measurable property of the resulting sentence, rather than merely a writing process.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas to ‘splice’ sentences

rules.quote: Don’t use a comma to link 2 stand-alone sentences unless you use a coordinating conjunction.
rules.violation_condition: A comma alone joins two stand-alone sentences without a coordinating conjunction.
when: Two stand-alone sentences are linked without a coordinating conjunction.
rules.why: G-4: consolidate the comma-splice heading with its explicit body definition.

covers.quote: Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas
This rule applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists.

rules.quote: Use commas between items in a sentence list.
rules.violation_condition: Items in an inline sentence list run together without the required separating commas.
when: Items form a list within a sentence or within a sentence fragment in a bullet list.
The comma before the final item is governed by the Oxford-comma conditions.
rules.why: G-1: mark the child rather than the grouping heading; G-4: use the precise body instruction. Final-item punctuation is consolidated with the Oxford-comma rule.

rules.quote: Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.
rules.violation_condition: A bullet-list item ends with a comma.
when: The item is in a bullet list.
rules.why: This checks terminal bullet punctuation, not separators inside a sentence list.

covers.quote: Avoid using a comma before the last item in the list.
If the last item combines 2 words or phrases with the word ‘and’, use a comma before that final item.
For example, use the Oxford comma before the last item if you’re using a defining phrase applicable only to that final item.

rules.quote: Restrict the use of the Oxford comma
rules.specification: Assess whether a final comma is needed to prevent ambiguity, including the two explicit cases. The page does not exhaustively define other complex-list ambiguities.
rules.violation_condition: A list has an unnecessary comma before its final item, or lacks that comma where the final item contains ‘and’ or where the comma is needed to disambiguate a defining phrase applying only to the final item.
when: Normally omit a comma before the last item in a sentence list.
Use it if the final item itself combines words or phrases with ‘and’.
Use it when a defining phrase applies only to the final item and omission would make its scope ambiguous.
An Oxford comma can prevent ambiguity in other complex sentence lists.
rules.why: G-2: the default omission and the two stated reasons for using a final comma are conditions of one check.

rules.quote: When writing strings of adjectives, use a set order – evaluative, descriptive, then definitive.
rules.violation_condition: A string of adjectives places descriptive adjectives before evaluative adjectives, or definitive adjectives before evaluative or descriptive adjectives.
when: A noun has a string of adjectives of different types.
rules.why: This is a distinct ordering check, not the same finding as adjective comma punctuation.

covers.quote: Separate adjectives of the same type
Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.

rules.quote: Use commas in strings of adjectives of the same type (for example, a string of descriptive adjectives).
rules.violation_condition: Adjacent adjectives of the same type lack a separating comma, or adjectives of different types are separated by a comma.
when: A noun has a string of adjectives.
Separate adjectives of the same type with commas.
Do not insert commas between adjectives of different types.
rules.why: G-2: same-type and different-type adjective boundaries are cases of one comma check; G-4: consolidate the heading.

covers.quote: Numbers with 4 or more digits (starting from 1,000) need a comma.
Use commas for numerals in text and in tables.
Don’t use a space between the digits, because screen readers can read them as separate numbers.
When you are using numbers of 1,000 or more, use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).
Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.
Don’t use commas in postcodes or dates.

rules.quote: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits
rules.violation_condition: A numeral has missing or misplaced thousands commas, uses spaces to group digits, or contains grouping commas in decimal digits, a date or a postcode.
when: Applies to numerals in running text and tables.
Group integer digits in threes from right to left for numbers of 1,000 or more.
Do not substitute spaces for grouping commas.
Do not group digits to the right of a decimal point with commas.
Do not use grouping commas in dates or postcodes.
rules.why: G-2: digit grouping, spaces, decimal digits, dates and postcodes are conditions of one numeric-punctuation check.

covers.quote: Use the comma in combination with quotation marks.

rules.quote: Introduce directly quoted speech with a comma.
rules.violation_condition: An introduction to directly quoted speech is not followed by a comma before the opening quotation mark.
when: Directly quoted speech follows its introduction or attribution.
rules.why: G-1: the heading groups several quotation-punctuation checks; use the specific body instruction.

rules.quote: If an attribution comes after a quotation, use a comma at the end of the quotation and before the quotation mark.
rules.specification: The page does not explain how this instruction interacts with quotations ending in question marks or exclamation marks. Those cases need review rather than an invented exception.
rules.violation_condition: A quotation followed by an attribution lacks a comma immediately inside its closing quotation mark, or puts that comma outside the mark.
when: An attribution follows a quotation.
rules.why: This checks punctuation before a following attribution, distinct from introducing a quotation.

rules.quote: If the quotation is broken into 2 parts, the second part should follow a full stop rather than a comma.
rules.specification: The examples resume the quotation with a new complete sentence. The wording does not clarify whether the instruction also applies when an attribution interrupts a single quoted sentence.
rules.violation_condition: The second part of a split quotation follows a comma after the attribution instead of a full stop.
when: A quotation is broken into two parts by an attribution.
rules.why: This is a distinct check on the boundary between the attribution and the resumed quotation.

rules.quote: If the quotation ends the sentence, end it with the original punctuation of the quotation.
rules.specification: Exact preservation requires access to the original quotation; sentence type can identify some likely errors but cannot establish the source punctuation in every case.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence-final quotation omits or changes the quotation’s original terminal punctuation.
when: The quotation ends the enclosing sentence.
rules.why: This is a distinct check on sentence-final quotation punctuation.

anchor.quote: Use a comma after introductory words, such as greetings and adverbs, or when addressing someone.

covers.quote: Place a comma after adverbs and other introductory words
You don’t need a comma after an introductory word if the sentence is very short.

tags.specification: The manual does not define ‘very short’. A checker needs a reviewer-approved interpretation of that exception.
tags.violation_condition: An introductory word, greeting or address is not separated from the following sentence by a comma, outside the very-short-sentence exception.

when: Applies to introductory words, greetings and words addressing someone.
A comma may be omitted if the sentence is very short.
rules.why: G-4: use the actionable body wording; G-3: retain the very-short-sentence permission as an exception.

anchor.quote: Use a comma after phrases and clauses that change the whole sentence

covers.quote: Use commas after adverbial phrases and adverbial clauses.
They should also have a comma after them if they start the sentence.
Use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral.
covers.suffix: It doesn’t matter how short the

covers.quote: It doesn’t matter how short the sentence is.
If ‘for example’ begins a sentence, it is an introductory phrase. Follow it with a comma.
In these cases, you don’t need a comma before the phrase.
covers.suffix: This simpler structure can be e

tags.violation_condition: An introductory phrase or clause is not separated from the main clause by a comma.

when: The phrase or clause introduces the sentence.
Includes conditional clauses beginning with words such as ‘if’, ‘unless’ or ‘until’.
Includes sentence-initial ‘for example’.
A comma is required between an introductory phrase ending with a numeral and an immediately following numeral, regardless of sentence length.
A phrase moved to the end of the sentence does not require a comma before it merely because it could have been introductory.
rules.why: G-2: introductory adverbial and conditional clauses and the numeral-boundary case are conditions of the same comma check.

anchor.quote: Avoid beginning a sentence with a string of numbers and dates

covers.quote: Avoid this type of sentence structure because the string of numbers can be confusing.

tags.specification: Flag the illustrated construction: an introductory date or number phrase immediately followed by another numeral, even if a comma separates them. Do not flag every sentence that merely begins with a date.
tags.violation_condition: A sentence begins with an introductory numeric or date phrase followed immediately by another numeral, creating a confusing string of numbers.

when: An introductory phrase ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral.
rules.why: G-4: the body restates this readability rule; the separate comma requirement is absorbed into the introductory-phrase rule.

anchor.quote: Use commas around clauses that add information but aren’t essential to the meaning of the sentence.

covers.quote: Set off non-essential clauses
Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.
If you can remove the clause and your sentence means the same thing, it’s non-essential and should go between commas.

tags.violation_condition: A non-essential clause lacks its delimiting commas, or an essential clause is incorrectly set off with commas.

when: Use delimiting commas for clauses that add non-essential information.
Do not delimit a clause with commas if it is essential to the intended meaning.
A clause is non-essential if removing it leaves the intended main meaning unchanged.
rules.why: G-1: mark the specific child rather than the grouping parent; G-2: essential and non-essential clauses are cases of the same clause-delimiting check.

anchor.quote: Use a pair of commas when you have 2 noun phrases next to each other that define the same thing.

covers.quote: Place commas around nouns that define the same thing they follow
You should be able to take out the noun phrase between the comma pair and still have a grammatically correct sentence.

tags.violation_condition: A supplementary noun phrase identifying the same thing as the preceding noun phrase is missing one or both delimiting commas.

when: Two adjacent noun phrases refer to the same thing and the second supplies non-essential information.
Removing the second noun phrase leaves a grammatically complete sentence.
rules.why: G-1: retain the specific apposition child; G-4: consolidate its heading and removal test.

anchor.prefix: gged onto the end of sentences.
anchor.quote: Use a comma before a question that is part of the sentence.

covers.quote: Separate questions tagged onto a sentence

tags.violation_condition: A question tag is attached to a sentence without a preceding comma.

when: A question tag is attached to the end of a sentence.
rules.why: G-1: question tags have their own specific check; G-4: use the actionable body sentence.

anchor.quote: Generally, use a comma before and after the phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence.

covers.quote: Use commas with the phrase ‘for example’

tags.specification: The manual says ‘Generally’ without enumerating all exceptions. The stated introductory and bullet-list cases are handled separately.
tags.violation_condition: Parenthetical ‘for example’ within a sentence lacks a comma before or after it.

when: ‘For example’ is parenthetical within a sentence.
Sentence-initial use follows the introductory-phrase rule.
Use before a bullet list follows the colon rule.
rules.why: G-4: choose the specific body wording; G-2: distinguish medial use from introductory and bullet-list uses.

anchor.quote: If you’re introducing a bullet list after ‘for example’, use a colon.

tags.violation_condition: A bullet-list lead-in ending in ‘for example’ lacks a colon after that phrase.

when: ‘For example’ introduces a bullet list.
rules.why: G-1: this is a distinct punctuation check, not a restatement of the surrounding comma rule.

anchor.quote: If you use Latin shortened forms, such as ‘e.g.’ and ‘i.e.’, don’t follow them with a comma.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas with Latin shortened forms

tags.violation_condition: A Latin shortened form is immediately followed by a comma.

when: A Latin shortened form such as ‘e.g.’ or ‘i.e.’ is used.
rules.why: G-4: the body specifies the position of the prohibited comma more precisely than the heading.

anchor.quote: Place commas between principal clauses joined together with a conjunction

covers.quote: Use commas to connect 2 or more principal clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’, ‘so’).
If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
The exception to this rule is when you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.

tags.violation_condition: Joined principal clauses lack a separating comma where their subjects differ, or a series of more than two shared-subject principal clauses lacks the required separating commas.

when: Principal clauses are joined by a coordinating conjunction such as ‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’ or ‘so’.
A comma is required before the conjunction when the clauses have different subjects.
Two clauses sharing one subject need neither a repeated subject nor a comma.
More than two principal clauses sharing one subject are separated with commas, including before the final conjunction.
rules.why: G-2: different subjects, a shared subject and more than two shared-subject clauses are conditions of one check.

anchor.quote: Do not use this rule to create a sentence of more than 25 words.

tags.violation_condition: A sentence formed by joining principal clauses with commas and coordinating conjunctions contains more than 25 words.

when: The sentence connects principal clauses using commas and coordinating conjunctions.
rules.why: The instruction gives a measurable property of the resulting sentence, rather than merely a writing process.

anchor.quote: Don’t use a comma to link 2 stand-alone sentences unless you use a coordinating conjunction.
anchor.suffix: This kind of error is called a

covers.quote: Don’t use commas to ‘splice’ sentences

tags.violation_condition: A comma alone joins two stand-alone sentences without a coordinating conjunction.

when: Two stand-alone sentences are linked without a coordinating conjunction.
rules.why: G-4: consolidate the comma-splice heading with its explicit body definition.

anchor.quote: Use commas between items in a sentence list.
anchor.suffix: Avoid using a comma before the

covers.quote: Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas
This rule applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists.
covers.suffix: Do not punctuate the end of a l

tags.violation_condition: Items in an inline sentence list run together without the required separating commas.

when: Items form a list within a sentence or within a sentence fragment in a bullet list.
The comma before the final item is governed by the Oxford-comma conditions.
rules.why: G-1: mark the child rather than the grouping heading; G-4: use the precise body instruction. Final-item punctuation is consolidated with the Oxford-comma rule.

anchor.quote: Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.

tags.violation_condition: A bullet-list item ends with a comma.

when: The item is in a bullet list.
rules.why: This checks terminal bullet punctuation, not separators inside a sentence list.

anchor.quote: Restrict the use of the Oxford comma

covers.prefix: tween items in a sentence list.
covers.quote: Avoid using a comma before the last item in the list.
If the last item combines 2 words or phrases with the word ‘and’, use a comma before that final item.
covers.suffix: This use of the comma is known

covers.quote: For example, use the Oxford comma before the last item if you’re using a defining phrase applicable only to that final item.

tags.specification: Assess whether a final comma is needed to prevent ambiguity, including the two explicit cases. The page does not exhaustively define other complex-list ambiguities.
tags.violation_condition: A list has an unnecessary comma before its final item, or lacks that comma where the final item contains ‘and’ or where the comma is needed to disambiguate a defining phrase applying only to the final item.

when: Normally omit a comma before the last item in a sentence list.
Use it if the final item itself combines words or phrases with ‘and’.
Use it when a defining phrase applies only to the final item and omission would make its scope ambiguous.
An Oxford comma can prevent ambiguity in other complex sentence lists.
rules.why: G-2: the default omission and the two stated reasons for using a final comma are conditions of one check.

anchor.quote: When writing strings of adjectives, use a set order – evaluative, descriptive, then definitive.

tags.violation_condition: A string of adjectives places descriptive adjectives before evaluative adjectives, or definitive adjectives before evaluative or descriptive adjectives.

when: A noun has a string of adjectives of different types.
rules.why: This is a distinct ordering check, not the same finding as adjective comma punctuation.

anchor.quote: Use commas in strings of adjectives of the same type (for example, a string of descriptive adjectives).

covers.quote: Separate adjectives of the same type
Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.

tags.violation_condition: Adjacent adjectives of the same type lack a separating comma, or adjectives of different types are separated by a comma.

when: A noun has a string of adjectives.
Separate adjectives of the same type with commas.
Do not insert commas between adjectives of different types.
rules.why: G-2: same-type and different-type adjective boundaries are cases of one comma check; G-4: consolidate the heading.

anchor.quote: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits

covers.quote: Numbers with 4 or more digits (starting from 1,000) need a comma.
covers.suffix: Use commas for numerals in text

covers.quote: Use commas for numerals in text and in tables.
Don’t use a space between the digits, because screen readers can read them as separate numbers.
When you are using numbers of 1,000 or more, use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).
Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.
Don’t use commas in postcodes or dates.

tags.violation_condition: A numeral has missing or misplaced thousands commas, uses spaces to group digits, or contains grouping commas in decimal digits, a date or a postcode.

when: Applies to numerals in running text and tables.
Group integer digits in threes from right to left for numbers of 1,000 or more.
Do not substitute spaces for grouping commas.
Do not group digits to the right of a decimal point with commas.
Do not use grouping commas in dates or postcodes.
rules.why: G-2: digit grouping, spaces, decimal digits, dates and postcodes are conditions of one numeric-punctuation check.

anchor.quote: Introduce directly quoted speech with a comma.
anchor.suffix: Use the comma in combination wi

covers.prefix: tly quoted speech with a comma.
covers.quote: Use the comma in combination with quotation marks.

tags.violation_condition: An introduction to directly quoted speech is not followed by a comma before the opening quotation mark.

when: Directly quoted speech follows its introduction or attribution.
rules.why: G-1: the heading groups several quotation-punctuation checks; use the specific body instruction.

anchor.quote: If an attribution comes after a quotation, use a comma at the end of the quotation and before the quotation mark.

tags.specification: The page does not explain how this instruction interacts with quotations ending in question marks or exclamation marks. Those cases need review rather than an invented exception.
tags.violation_condition: A quotation followed by an attribution lacks a comma immediately inside its closing quotation mark, or puts that comma outside the mark.

when: An attribution follows a quotation.
rules.why: This checks punctuation before a following attribution, distinct from introducing a quotation.

anchor.quote: If the quotation is broken into 2 parts, the second part should follow a full stop rather than a comma.

tags.specification: The examples resume the quotation with a new complete sentence. The wording does not clarify whether the instruction also applies when an attribution interrupts a single quoted sentence.
tags.violation_condition: The second part of a split quotation follows a comma after the attribution instead of a full stop.

when: A quotation is broken into two parts by an attribution.
rules.why: This is a distinct check on the boundary between the attribution and the resumed quotation.

anchor.quote: If the quotation ends the sentence, end it with the original punctuation of the quotation.

tags.specification: Exact preservation requires access to the original quotation; sentence type can identify some likely errors but cannot establish the source punctuation in every case.
tags.violation_condition: A sentence-final quotation omits or changes the quotation’s original terminal punctuation.

when: The quotation ends the enclosing sentence.
rules.why: This is a distinct check on sentence-final quotation punctuation.
